Last summer I did a one-month homestay in Osaka. My host family was three people: the father, the mother, and Yui, a high school student.
On the first day I was very nervous. But the mother said, "Think of this as your own home," so I felt relieved.
Yui is in the cooking club at school. On weekends, Yui taught me Japanese home cooking. The dish I liked most was nikujaga.
After I went back to my country, I tried making nikujaga for my family. But it tasted a little different from what I ate in Japan. Next time I meet Yui, I plan to ask her again how to make it.

reading.en:
Club Activities in Japan, by Li Min
It has been half a year since I came to study at a Japanese high school. What surprised me most at school in Japan was club activities. Schools in my country also have sports and music clubs, but they only practice once or twice a week. In Japan, many clubs practice every day, and some even practice on Saturdays and Sundays.
At first I wanted to join the soccer club. But the soccer club practices every morning and evening, and I thought I would have no time to study, so I gave up. Then a friend invited me, and I joined the tea ceremony club, which practices three times a week.
In the tea ceremony club we learn not only how to make tea but also greetings and how to sit. At first my legs hurt and it was hard, but now I can stay seated for about thirty minutes. Next month, at the school festival, we will serve tea to guests. My family is coming from my country to watch, so I am practicing hard.
